title: File and folder permissions in each system

videos.script: The payroll spreadsheet lives in a shared folder on the office server. The accountant needs to change it, and the partners need to read it. The new intern, who helps with invoices in the folder next door, should not be able to open it at all. {{payroll}} That is what permissions are: the operating system's answer, file by file, to who may read, who may change, and who may run or enter. Nothing on a shared computer is private or shared by accident. It is exactly as open as its permissions say. {{answer}} Linux and macOS ask the same three questions for three kinds of people: the owner, one group, and everybody else. Windows keeps a list instead, as long as it needs to be, with an entry for anybody. The two models solve the same problem and fail in different ways. {{models}} You will read a Linux permission string, and see what each letter really allows on a file and on a folder. You will change permissions by letter and by number, and set up a folder a whole group can share. Then you will read a Windows access control list, and see where macOS sits between the two. {{steps}} The Linux transcripts come from lesson 3's server, with two extra users to test each permission from the other side. The Windows and macOS commands are shown, not run. {{honest}}
